\documentclass[11pt]{article}
\usepackage[margin=1in]{geometry}
\usepackage{graphicx}
\usepackage{booktabs}

\title{Phenological Shifts in Alpine Meadows:\\Eight Years of Warming-Experiment Evidence}
\author{L.~Bergmann, T.~Nakamura, and F.~Ricci}
\date{April 2026}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Alpine meadows are warming faster than the global average, and their
flowering phenology is among the most sensitive biological indicators of
climate change. We report eight years of phenological records from a
warming experiment with open-top chambers replicated across an elevation
gradient in the central Alps. Flowering advanced by 2.1 days per year on
control plots and by 3.4 days per year on warmed plots, and the
community-weighted mean flowering date shifted earlier at all sites.
The advance was strongest at the highest site, where snowmelt timing,
rather than air temperature during the growing season, explained most of
the interannual variance.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
The timing of flowering determines the length of the growing season,
the overlap between plants and their pollinators, and the exposure of
reproductive organs to late frost. Warming experiments have documented
phenological sensitivity across many biomes, but alpine studies with
both experimental warming and an elevation gradient remain rare.

Here we analyse eight complete growing seasons from a replicated
experiment in the central Alps. Three meadow sites at 1900, 2200, and
2500~m elevation each host twelve plots, half of them warmed with
open-top chambers. The design lets us separate experimental warming from
the background trend, and the elevation gradient lets us ask whether
sensitivity increases with elevation, as snowmelt-driven hypotheses
predict.

\section{Study Area and Design}
The experiment occupies three south-facing meadows on calcareous
bedrock. Figure~\ref{fig:map} shows the study area and the sampling
sites along the elevation gradient.
\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\IfFileExists{figures/trait_means.pdf}{\includegraphics[width=0.75\textwidth]{figures/trait_means.pdf}}{\rule{0.75\textwidth}{4.5cm}}
\caption{Community-weighted mean trait values across elevations.}
\label{fig:traits}
\end{figure}
The three sites share the same bedrock and grazing history but differ in
mean annual temperature by roughly 1.1~$^\circ$C per 300~m step. Each
site hosts twelve 2~m$\times$2~m plots arranged in six pairs, with one
plot of each pair assigned to warming and the other to control. The
open-top chambers raise the growing-season mean air temperature by
1.4~$^\circ$C on average, a magnitude chosen to match regional
projections for mid-century.

Vegetation is dominated by sedges and forbs typical of subalpine and
alpine grassland, with 38 species recorded over the eight years. Sheep
grazing continues on all sites in late summer, following the historical
management of the valley.

\section{Phenological Records}
Every plot was censused twice weekly from the day of snowmelt, defined
as the first day with less than 10\% snow cover, to the first autumn
frost. For each species present in a plot, we recorded the date of first
open flower and the date of peak flowering, defined as the census with
the maximum number of open flowers. Censuses were conducted by the same
two observers throughout, and a cross-calibration exercise every spring
kept observer bias below one day for the common species.

Community-level flowering dates were computed as abundance-weighted
means of the species-level dates, using visual cover estimates as
weights. The weighting matters in these meadows because a small number
of abundant sedges flower early and would otherwise be drowned out by
the many rare forbs that flower in mid-season. Analyses at the species
level use linear mixed models with plot as a random effect; community
analyses use the plot-level weighted means directly.

Snow depth and melt-out date were recorded at each plot with time-lapse
cameras and weekly stake readings, so that every census year has a
plot-specific snowmelt date. Soil temperature at 5~cm depth was logged
hourly on four plots per site, and the degree-day series enter the
species models as covariates.

Missing data are rare but structured: two plots at the highest site were
buried by a late avalanche in 2021 and censused only from July onward.
Those plot-years are excluded from the community-level trend estimates,
and sensitivity analyses that impute the missing early season produce
trends within 0.2 days per year of those reported below.

\section{Results}
Flowering advanced over the eight years at all three sites and in both
treatments. On control plots the community-weighted mean flowering date
advanced by 2.1 days per year, and on warmed plots by 3.4 days per year,
with the difference between treatments significant at all sites. The
advance was fastest at the highest site, where the control trend was
3.0 days per year and the warmed trend 4.6 days per year.

The interannual variance in flowering date was dominated by snowmelt
timing at the highest site, where snowmelt alone explained 71\% of the
variance, and by early-season air temperature at the lowest site, where
temperature in the four weeks after snowmelt explained 58\%. The
warmed--control difference in flowering date was largest in years with
late snowmelt, suggesting that the chambers amplify the phenological
consequences of winter conditions rather than simply adding a constant
offset.

The first flowering date of the earliest species, a sedge that flowers
within days of melt-out, advanced almost one-for-one with snowmelt at
all sites, whereas the peak flowering date of the community advanced
more slowly, so that the flowering season lengthened over the record.
This lengthening is visible in the census data as a growing gap between
the first and the peak flowering dates, and it is strongest on the
warmed plots at the two higher sites.

Trait composition shifted alongside phenology. Figure~\ref{fig:traits}
reports the community-weighted mean trait values across the elevation
gradient for the first and last four years of the experiment.
\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\IfFileExists{figures/site_map.pdf}{\includegraphics[width=0.75\textwidth]{figures/site_map.pdf}}{\rule{0.75\textwidth}{4.5cm}}
\caption{Study area and sampling sites along the elevation gradient.}
\label{fig:map}
\end{figure}
Specific leaf area increased significantly on warmed plots at all sites,
consistent with a shift toward faster-growing species, while leaf dry
matter content declined. Plant height increased only at the lowest site,
where competition for light is strongest.

Species-level responses were heterogeneous. Of the 21 species with
sufficient data, 16 advanced their flowering significantly under warming,
three showed no response, and two late-flowering composites delayed
slightly. The two delaying species also declined in cover on warmed
plots, suggesting that phenological inflexibility carries a competitive
cost under the new regime.

\section{Discussion}
The elevation pattern of phenological sensitivity supports the view
that snowmelt timing is the master variable of alpine phenology, and
that warming acts on flowering largely by advancing snowmelt and
extending the season. This reconciles our results with the weaker
sensitivities reported from lower-elevation grasslands, where snow
plays no role and photoperiod constrains the earliest flowering.

The trait shifts we document suggest that the phenological advance is
not merely plastic: the community is changing in composition toward
species with faster strategies, which implies that the observed advance
will persist even if the warming trend pauses. The decline of the two
phenologically inflexible species is an early warning that not all
components of these communities can track the shifting season.

Our conclusions are bounded by the chamber method, which warms the air
but not the deep soil, and by the elevation gradient, which partly
confounds temperature with management history.

\section{Conclusion}
Eight years of replicated warming across an elevation gradient show
that alpine meadow flowering is advancing rapidly, that the advance is
fastest where snow dominates the phenological calendar, and that the
community is restructuring toward faster-growing species. The released
dataset offers a rare long window onto the reordering of alpine
communities under warming.
\end{document}
